summary:

I explicitly tell it to look at the code in the context, then I start to realize it's making generalizations. "oh yeah, I should have answered from the code!"

The frustrating aspect is that the items listed above are like models from 6-12 months ago. Astra is absolutely amazing and shouldn't perform this way.

title: Tell HN: Google Search to start locking down search behind a login wall
summary:
Usually, when I used Google Search on some ISP CGNAT IP addresses (not even a VPN), I usually get countless CAPTCHAs evertime I initiate a new session to Google Search on a new private browsing window (probably an artifact from residential proxy botnets).

Recently, in addition to that, they started to just lock the entire search results page behind a login prompt on some of those bad IP addresses (like YouTube does for some time with the "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot" prompt). This potentially makes the service less accessible, especially for those using a shared/public computers.

I did not even get this prompt on some VPN IPs, and even no CAPTCHAs at all, even with a free one like given by Firefox.

Has anyone encountered that? I just encountered this today. It's really unfortunate for the internet to become less friendly to signed-out users, especially since AI scrapers starting to "abuse" the internet for their value.

title: Using LLMs outside of reflection is an anti-pattern
summary:
LLMs have a great deal of value in that they are the world's most advanced rubber duck.[1]

They contain all of the references[2] from Google + the ability to somewhat encourage self-evaluation and reflection. However in terms of patterns/anti-patterns, the use of LLMs to create code without human interaction is itself an emerging anti-pattern. Just like any bit of code that functions despite being a form of pasta[3], an anti-pattern doesn't mean things won't function... but you are guaranteed to bake-in a certain level of performance loss and general negative quirkiness; just like in cases of programming in regards to date & time-zones, the devil is in the details and often appears years down the line, not right away.

The fruit of the LLM tree is made more tempting by taking away part of what creates good code: the difficulty. Difficult games or experiences create people who are capable of handling deviations from standard running procedures and anticipate failure upstream. This isn't possible with a LLM structure because the whole aim is reducing the difficulty of production and increasing speed.

Consider the example of the Luddite[4], where the artisan weaver is replaced by a leap in industrialization: this isn't so much the case with a LLM. They work faster, but with far less accuracy. Imagine a rug weaved together in minutes with no discernible pattern. Certainly under the supervision of an expert this improves but imperfections emerge in the system that require a halt of the speed, rollbacks that eat away at production time and create vast effects in terms of customer opinion of the process and the product.

Not to use LLMs at all is likely folly. Knowing how to use them well will be the difference between the master and the apprentice.[5]

Hopefully more identification of LLM patterns and anti-patterns will begin to evolve along with what seems to be another new release from Pandora's Box.[6]

[2] https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/03/google-search-artificial-intelligence

[5] https://disney.fandom.com/wiki/ The_Sorcerer%27s_Apprentice

title: Ask HN: Has AI coding changed who builds your internal tools?
summary:
In a large company, a dedicated team might build an internal tool that dozens of other teams use. If your team needs a feature for its own workflow, you have to explain the use case, agree on how it fits into the shared tool, and wait for it to get prioritised. With AI coding tools, it might now be faster for the team that needs the feature to build and maintain its own tool or completely scratch the tool and rebuild it if need. I’m curious how that plays out once the tool has been in use for a while. So is paradigm shifting where we remove centralisation of building internal tools and let teams decide?

title: Ask HN: How do you upgrade the models you run in production?
summary:
Hi! I'm an AI engineer at a Series D company. We use LLMs for basically everything: customer responses, classification, routing, clustering, etc. While most of my focus is on developing new features, writing evals for them and monitoring quality in production, I can't help but look for opportunities to improve our current ways of doing things. One of these is model upgrades. It seems that we keep models until OpenAI decides to deprecate them, whereas everyone knows that we could have saved money and made better product by making the switch earlier on. Another adjacent problem is over reliance on LLMs to do everything where as a simpler classifier could have sufficed. So I have a couple of questions for my fellow ai engineers

- When did you last switch models, and what triggered it?

- How did you check the new model didn't regress? Eval suite, replaying real traffic, spot checks, just shipping it?

- Have you ever moved a task to a smaller model? an open source one ? What made you do it?

- Is there anything you run on an LLM that a classifier or plain rules could handle?

title: Treating web animations as editable clips in a video timeline
summary:
A web animation can play in a browser. But putting it in a video timeline requires more than a play button: you need to trim it, move it, duplicate it, and jump directly to a particular moment.

In Breatic, we represent each web-animation clip with a position on the timeline, an in-point in the original animation, and a duration. Trimming changes those values while leaving the animation’s source intact.

For example, take a 10-second animation and keep only seconds 3–6. Place that clip at second 20 of the timeline. When the playhead reaches second 21, the animation needs to show its original second 4.

At normal playback speed, the mapping is:

*Animation time = source in-point + timeline time − clip start*

The animation runtime must support rendering at a requested time. This works with animations prepared for our playback runtime; it doesn’t make an arbitrary web page seekable.

There is another detail: sending a seek request doesn’t mean the new frame is ready to display. Our preview runs the animation inside an iframe. After applying a seek, the page waits for fonts and two animation frames before acknowledging the request. Session and sequence identifiers prevent an outdated response from satisfying a newer seek.

The latest Timeline changes add layered preview playback and controls to move, resize, and rotate video and web-animation layers. Combined with the existing trimming support, this lets the same animation appear in several independently edited clips alongside video.

These changes are merged into the main branch but haven’t shipped in a new release yet. This currently covers editing and preview; video export is still future work.

Source: https://github.com/orime-org/breatic
